Trying to Conceive

Diabetes, fertility and pregnancy: a plan for both partners

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Diabetes does not automatically prevent pregnancy. It can affect sexual function, sperm, ovulation and pregnancy health, but those are different questions with different investigations. A useful plan considers both partners, the type of diabetes, current treatment and other possible fertility factors. Improving health can reduce some risks without guaranteeing conception or a particular pregnancy outcome.

Start with both partners, not a verdict from one diagnosis

Many people with diabetes become parents. If pregnancy is taking longer than expected, do not assume that diabetes explains everything or that the partner without diabetes needs no assessment. Age, ovulation, sperm delivery and production, the fallopian tubes and other conditions can all matter. A blood glucose result can help assess diabetes; it cannot identify the precise cause of a couple’s fertility difficulty.

Ask your diabetes clinician about family plans before trying to conceive, and raise sexual symptoms without embarrassment. Bring both partners’ relevant history, medicines and previous results to a fertility appointment. There is no established “fertility cleanse” that removes diabetes-related reproductive risk. Avoid replacing necessary care with a supplement, restrictive diet or an online promise of a quick cure.

Type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes are not interchangeable

Type 1 diabetes usually involves an immune attack on the insulin-producing cells. Insulin treatment is essential; it is not a condition that can be managed by simply avoiding sugar. Type 2 diabetes involves reduced responsiveness to insulin and insufficient insulin production for the body’s needs. It can require medicines or insulin as well as practical nutrition and activity support, and is not necessarily mild.

Gestational diabetes is diagnosed during pregnancy in someone who did not previously have established diabetes. It is a separate situation from entering pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. Neither stress nor body weight alone explains every diagnosis. Avoid ranking one type as universally the most dangerous: treatment, complications, glucose patterns and the individual pregnancy determine the care needed.

Erections, ejaculation and sperm delivery

Diabetes-related nerve or blood-vessel damage can contribute to erection difficulties. Medicines, hormones, other illnesses, pain, emotional strain and relationship factors may also contribute. Delayed ejaculation, inability to ejaculate or retrograde ejaculation can reduce the chance of sperm reaching the vagina even when sperm are being produced. Little or no outward semen after orgasm, or cloudy urine afterwards, can prompt assessment for retrograde ejaculation, in which semen travels into the bladder.

A clinician can review the history, examination and relevant tests rather than treating every problem as low sperm count. Selected cases need a urine sample after ejaculation or a fertility/urology referral. Treatment may address sexual function or sperm delivery, and specialists can discuss assisted conception when appropriate. Do not start testosterone as a fertility booster: external testosterone can suppress sperm production, even if it improves some symptoms of low testosterone.

What the often-quoted sperm-DNA study actually found

A small 2007 study compared 27 men with diabetes with 29 men without diabetes who were undergoing infertility investigations. Average semen volume was 2.6 versus 3.3 mL; the other conventional semen measures did not differ significantly. Nuclear sperm-DNA fragmentation averaged 53% versus 32%, and the median number of mitochondrial DNA deletions was four versus three.

Those are laboratory findings in a particular study, not a fertility prediction for every man with diabetes. The fragmentation difference was 21 percentage points, not “20% more DNA.” The study did not measure an individual’s miscarriage, birth-defect or live-birth probability. A specialist should interpret actual semen results and the couple’s circumstances; this paper alone does not justify routine DNA-fragmentation testing for everyone with diabetes.

Paternal diabetes and pregnancy outcomes: what remains uncertain

Damage measured in a sperm test is not the same as proving harm to a future baby. A Danish assisted-reproduction cohort published online in 2024 did not find a statistically significant reduction in pregnancy or live-birth outcomes with paternal diabetes, but estimates were imprecise and the findings concern people receiving that treatment. A separate US claims study associated a father’s metabolic health problems with pregnancy loss; this observational association cannot establish that diabetes caused a loss.

A 2026 Danish study found that the assessed outcomes with paternal type 1 diabetes were broadly comparable with the general population after adjustment, whereas maternal type 1 diabetes carried greater risks. It examined outcomes such as prematurity and birth size, not every possible outcome or congenital abnormality. Together these studies support an honest discussion of uncertainty, not a blanket claim that paternal diabetes either causes fetal malformations or has no possible reproductive effects.

Female fertility, cycles and other conditions

Diabetes can coexist with irregular ovulation, sexual discomfort and other conditions affecting conception. Higher body weight and insulin resistance may overlap with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, previously called polycystic ovary syndrome or PCOS. Having diabetes does not itself establish that diagnosis. Pain, vaginal dryness or reduced desire can also make intercourse difficult and deserve care rather than blame.

A Swedish register study of women with type 2 diabetes found more recorded infertility and miscarriage and fewer births than in its comparison group. It was observational and cannot provide an individual loss percentage or prove the mechanism. It does not support claims that someone becomes pregnant every month but cannot implant an embryo, or that all people with diabetes face a 30–60% miscarriage rate. Irregular or absent periods warrant an individualized investigation.

Choose tests for the question being asked

Fertility evaluation usually starts with both partners’ histories, assessment of ovulation and a semen analysis when relevant. Examination, tubal assessment, hormone tests or other investigations follow the findings. AUA/ASRM guidance does not recommend sperm-DNA fragmentation as a routine initial test. It can have a selected role, for example in some recurrent pregnancy-loss or assisted-treatment assessments; diabetes alone is not a universal indication.

Type 1 diabetes and other autoimmune conditions can coexist, but this does not prove thyroid disease, premature ovarian insufficiency or early menopause in a particular person. Diabetes-specific preconception care can include thyroid testing. In a general fertility assessment, thyroid and reproductive hormone tests should follow the clinical context: FSH and estradiol may help investigate absent periods, for example. An automatic TSH/FSH panel cannot settle every fertility question or replace interpreting symptoms and results together.

When to arrange fertility assessment

Arrange preconception diabetes care before trying, regardless of how long you have been trying to conceive. For fertility investigation, ASRM generally advises assessment after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse when the egg-producing partner is under 35, or after six months at 35 or older. Over 40, an earlier assessment may be appropriate. Local referral arrangements and individual circumstances can differ.

Do not wait for those intervals if there are irregular or absent periods, known reproductive problems, concerning semen results or sexual difficulties that prevent conception. Evaluate both partners in parallel where applicable. A fertility referral need not mean that IVF is required; the next step depends on the identified problem, age, preferences and the time available. Ask for a plan that coordinates the fertility and diabetes teams.

Before conception, agree safe glucose goals

Glucose control before conception matters because early development occurs before many people know they are pregnant. NICE and ADA use an HbA1c goal below 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) before conception when this can be achieved safely, without problematic hypoglycaemia. HbA1c reflects longer-term glucose exposure; it is not the same measurement as a current finger-prick glucose reading.

The team should help set realistic targets, monitoring and treatment changes. A very high HbA1c needs prompt specialist planning; NICE advises avoiding conception while HbA1c is above 10% (86 mmol/mol) until it is lowered. Discuss contraception if you wish to defer pregnancy while improving control, without treating a target as a judgement about you. Any improvement may help, and a result below target cannot guarantee a complication-free pregnancy.

Review medicines and folic acid before trying

Do not stop essential insulin or change diabetes treatment on your own. Some glucose, blood-pressure and cholesterol medicines need replacement or a planned pause before pregnancy; others may remain appropriate. The team must arrange effective treatment while making changes. US ADA guidance prefers insulin for type 2 diabetes in pregnancy, while UK NICE permits selected metformin use when benefits outweigh potential harm. Your actual prescription, including any combination tablet, needs an individual review.

Ask which folic acid recommendation applies where you receive care. UK NICE recommends prescribed 5 mg daily for women with diabetes planning pregnancy until 12 weeks; US ADA preconception guidance describes prenatal folic acid of 400–800 micrograms daily. These are different guideline approaches, not instructions to combine products or choose the highest dose yourself. Bring supplements and all medicine packaging, including weight-management treatments, to the review.

Check complications and make the plan workable

Preconception assessment includes eye and kidney health, blood pressure and other relevant conditions. Retinal assessment is particularly important before rapidly improving glucose control when retinopathy may be present. Kidney function and urine protein findings can influence pregnancy monitoring and medicines. Ask which checks are due, what any abnormal result means and whether a specialist review is needed before conception.

A sustainable plan also covers food access, activity, tobacco or alcohol concerns, sleep, emotional wellbeing and the cost of medicines or monitoring supplies. Seek individualized nutrition advice rather than a crash diet or blame about weight. Agree whom to contact outside clinic hours and how fertility treatment, pregnancy care and diabetes follow-up will communicate. Write down the next appointment and what information to bring.

After a positive test, contact the team promptly

An unexpected pregnancy is a reason for prompt diabetes and maternity advice, not panic or self-directed treatment withdrawal. Provide the test date, current medicines, glucose information and any symptoms. Poorly controlled maternal diabetes can increase miscarriage and congenital-abnormality risks, especially around conception, and can affect fetal growth and later pregnancy. Care aims to lower these risks while preventing severe low glucose.

The monitoring plan may include review of eye or kidney disease, fetal assessment and growth monitoring, and individualized decisions about birth and newborn care. A normal scan does not answer every question, and diabetes does not mean that loss or malformation is inevitable. Ask which risks apply to your circumstances rather than relying on a single internet percentage. The medication and monitoring plan may need adjustment as pregnancy progresses.

The baby’s glucose exposure is different from inherited susceptibility

When the pregnant person has diabetes, high glucose reaching the fetus can stimulate fetal insulin production and contribute to a larger baby. After birth, that insulin effect can cause low newborn glucose. Some babies also develop jaundice, a high red-cell count or breathing problems; growth restriction can occur in other circumstances. These are reasons for an individualized newborn feeding and monitoring plan, not outcomes that every baby will develop.

A father’s diabetes does not expose the fetus to high maternal blood glucose by the same pathway. Either parent can contribute inherited susceptibility to diabetes, but genes are not the whole explanation and a child is not certain to develop it. Newborn low glucose is not proof that the baby has inherited diabetes. Ask the team to separate family-history questions from pregnancy exposure and the baby’s immediate clinical needs.

High glucose, illness and ketoacidosis need a clear response

Ask for written sick-day and ketone instructions, especially with type 1 diabetes, and do not simply omit insulin because you are eating less. Contact the team urgently for high readings that are not responding to your agreed treatment, concerning ketones or difficulty managing illness. Pregnancy can bring diabetic ketoacidosis at lower glucose levels than usual, so a glucose reading that is not extremely high cannot rule it out.

Suspected ketoacidosis needs emergency assessment. Possible symptoms include vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, fruity-smelling breath, unusual drowsiness or confusion; thirst and frequent urination can also occur. Do not wait for every sign or extremely high glucose. Seek emergency help directly and do not drive yourself.

Prepare for low glucose and keep support available

Insulin and some other diabetes medicines can cause low glucose. If you are awake and able to swallow safely, follow your agreed plan for fast-acting carbohydrate and rechecking; the NHS general advice is to recheck after 10–15 minutes. Repeated episodes need a treatment review. Tell someone close to you how to recognize a low and where your supplies are kept, particularly while preparing for or going through pregnancy.

If a person is unconscious or cannot swallow safely, give nothing by mouth. Call for emergency help when they are not responding normally or are unconscious, place a breathing person in the recovery position, and use prescribed glucagon only if available and you know how. Do not leave them alone. Once an episode is resolved, review its cause and prevention with the diabetes team rather than stopping insulin or abandoning pregnancy plans without advice.

Turn the next appointment into a shared plan

Bring your diabetes type, treatment list, recent glucose or HbA1c results, cycle or sexual symptoms, previous pregnancies and how long you have been trying. Ask what needs attention before conception, whether both partners need fertility investigations, what changes after a positive test and how to obtain urgent advice. If a suggested test or treatment is costly, ask what question it answers and how its result would change care.

Managing diabetes and fertility together can be tiring. Support for anxiety, sexual concerns, grief after loss or practical access difficulties is part of care. BeMama can help keep your questions and clinician-issued plans together; it cannot diagnose infertility or estimate an individual baby’s risk from a sperm or glucose result. A clear follow-up date and named contact are more useful than a promise that perfect control guarantees a baby.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Book a preconception review and bring both partners’ relevant history, medicines and previous fertility results.

Ask the clinician to write down the glucose targets, medicine and folate plan, required eye/kidney checks and what to do after a positive pregnancy test.

Keep sick-day, ketone and low-glucose instructions with an urgent contact number, and teach a trusted person the agreed emergency steps.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps organize glucose records, prescribed medicines, cycle or sexual symptoms, appointment questions and the team’s written plans. It cannot diagnose infertility, interpret sperm-DNA results as a baby’s prognosis, select diabetes treatment or calculate a personal pregnancy risk. Use clinical services directly for urgent symptoms.

When to seek help

Do not stop essential insulin or change treatment without an appropriate clinical plan. Suspected ketoacidosis requires emergency assessment even without extremely high glucose or every symptom. If someone is unresponsive or unconscious with suspected low glucose, summon emergency help and give nothing by mouth; use prescribed glucagon only if available and you know how. Do not drive yourself during a suspected diabetic emergency. Contact the diabetes/maternity team promptly after a positive pregnancy test.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Diabetes can affect fertility in either partner, but does not automatically make pregnancy impossible.
  • Semen laboratory findings, paternal pregnancy outcomes and maternal glucose exposure are different kinds of evidence.
  • Investigate both partners as appropriate; do not assume one diagnosis explains every fertility difficulty.
  • Arrange preconception glucose, medicine, folate, eye and kidney planning without stopping necessary treatment yourself.
  • A positive pregnancy test needs prompt team contact, and suspected ketoacidosis or severe hypoglycaemia needs emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

Can a couple conceive if one partner has diabetes?

Yes, many do. Diabetes may affect sexual function, sperm, ovulation or pregnancy health, but is not an automatic infertility diagnosis. Preconception diabetes care and, when needed, assessment of both partners help identify the relevant issues. A single glucose test cannot explain every difficulty conceiving.

How can diabetes affect male fertility?

Nerve and blood-vessel effects can contribute to erections or ejaculation difficulties; some people also have abnormal semen findings. Other conditions and medicines may matter. Little outward semen or cloudy urine after orgasm can prompt assessment for retrograde ejaculation. Do not take testosterone to improve fertility, because it can suppress sperm production.

Does diabetes always damage sperm DNA?

No. A small 2007 study found higher average DNA fragmentation in its diabetes group, but this does not describe every person or measure a future baby’s outcome. Semen analysis and clinical history usually come first; DNA-fragmentation testing is selected, not routine for everyone with diabetes.

Does a father’s diabetes cause miscarriage or birth defects?

It is not justified to make that blanket claim. Some observational paternal-health studies find associations, while other studies of particular treatment or pregnancy outcomes are reassuring. They examine different populations and cannot guarantee every outcome. Sperm-DNA findings alone do not establish that paternal diabetes caused a loss or malformation.

Do all women with diabetes need thyroid and FSH tests?

Testing depends on the question. Diabetes-specific preconception care can include thyroid assessment, while general fertility testing is guided by symptoms, cycle history and findings. FSH and other hormones can help investigate absent periods but are not a universal fertility screen. Diabetes does not automatically mean PMOS/PCOS or premature ovarian insufficiency.

What should I do before trying or after a positive test?

Arrange a diabetes/preconception review before trying, or contact the team promptly after a positive test. Discuss safe glucose targets, medicines, folic acid, eyes, kidneys and pregnancy monitoring. Guidelines differ on some medicine and folate choices; do not select a regimen online or stop insulin while waiting for an appointment.

Will the baby inherit diabetes?

Parental diabetes can contribute to susceptibility, but inheritance is not certain and other factors matter. This differs from effects of high maternal glucose during pregnancy. A newborn’s low glucose, jaundice or need for monitoring does not by itself mean the baby has inherited diabetes.

Which diabetes symptoms cannot wait?

Suspected ketoacidosis needs emergency care, with possible symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, fruity breath, unusual drowsiness or confusion; do not wait for every sign or extremely high glucose. For an unresponsive or unconscious person with suspected low glucose, summon emergency help and give nothing by mouth; use prescribed glucagon only if available and you know how. Follow the sick-day plan and do not simply stop insulin.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
